name: Vermis
summary: The narrow midline ridge joining the two hemispheres, folded into ten lobules from the lingula at the top to the nodule at the bottom. Together with the adjacent paravermis it forms the spinocerebellum, receiving proprioceptive information from the trunk and limbs and vestibular input, and projecting through the fastigial nuclei to the vestibular nuclei and reticular formation. It governs posture, gait, trunk stability and eye movements, which is why midline disease presents with truncal ataxia and nystagmus rather than limb dysmetria. It is also the part most damaged by alcohol and the usual seat of childhood medulloblastoma.

anatomy.location: Midline of the cerebellum between the hemispheres, forming the roof of the fourth ventricle inferiorly; its lobules (I–X) are numbered from the superior surface (lingula) around the posterior surface to the nodule in front of the uvula.

subdivisions.name: Superior vermis (I–V)
subdivisions.note: anterior lobe; trunk and leg proprioception; alcohol-related degeneration

subdivisions.name: Posterior vermis (VI–VIII)
subdivisions.note: declive, folium, tuber, pyramid; ocular motor vermis (VI–VII) controls saccade accuracy

subdivisions.name: Uvula and nodule (IX–X)
subdivisions.note: vestibulocerebellum with the flocculus; balance and vestibulo-ocular reflex adaptation

function: Postural and gait control, trunk stability, muscle tone of axial muscles, saccade accuracy and pursuit; relays through the fastigial nucleus.

bestView.label: midline vermis: all lobules on one sagittal slice

imaging.normalAppearance: Best seen on the midline sagittal T1, where the primary fissure separates the anterior from the posterior lobe and the folia of each lobule can be counted. Superior vermian atrophy is the hallmark of alcoholic cerebellar degeneration.

pathology.finding: Atrophy of the superior vermis with widened interfolial spaces on sagittal T1.
Midline mass of the inferior vermis bulging into the fourth ventricle with restricted diffusion (dense cells) and hydrocephalus, typically in a child.
Restricted diffusion in the superior (SCA) or inferior (PICA) vermis.

lesionEffects.deficit: Truncal ataxia: unable to sit unsupported, wide-based gait
Gaze-evoked and downbeat nystagmus, inaccurate saccades
Titubation of the head and trunk

examination: Watch the patient sit unsupported and walk heel-to-toe
Romberg: cerebellar patients cannot stand feet together even with eyes open
pearls: Alcohol spares the hands and ruins the gait because it attacks the superior vermis
A child with morning headache, vomiting and truncal ataxia has a midline posterior fossa tumor until proven otherwise

pitfalls: In the public edition the vermis is not the non-commercial probabilistic cerebellar atlas but a segmentation of the MNI152NLin2009cAsym template itself, made here with FastSurfer's CerebNet module (Apache-2.0 software; the five `cerebellar-vermis-*-fs` meshes), and CerebNet's vermis is coarser than the private edition's eight parcels: it names VI, VII (crus I, crus II and VIIb together), VIII (VIIIa and VIIIb together), IX and X. Dice against the private-edition vermis is 0.87 for VI, 0.74 for VII, 0.78 for VIII, 0.71 for IX and 0.69 for X, so the vermian strips are the least certain surfaces in that edition — read them as the position of the vermian lobule, not as its exact width.
